O PREFACE O We are living in an age where Science and Technology shape nearly every dimension of human life. From the way we communicate to the way we learn, work, and solve problems, technology has become deeply woven into our daily existence and Computer Science stands at the very heart of this transformation. This is the first time that Computer Science textbooks for Grade XI and Grade XII are being published separately, allowing each book to be developed with greater focus and depth suited to its respective grade level. These textbooks have also been aligned with the National Curriculum of Computer Science 2023 developed by National Curriculum Council (NCC), ensuring that students across the country learn from a consistent, nationally recognized standard. As updated textbooks, they provide students with new and relevant content, keeping pace with the rapid and multidirectional developments taking place across all branches of science. This Computer Science textbook for Grade XI has been developed in line with the revised curriculum and reviewed by an independent team from the Directorate of Curriculum Assessment and Research, Jamshoro. Recognizing the growing significance of Computer Science in today's world, its content has been thoughtfully restructured to'meet the evolving needs of learners. These features have been incorporated to spark curiosity, deepenunderstanding, and guide students toward future academic and professional pathways, while also enhancing the overall usefulness of the book for both students and teachers. First, how computers store and process information using simple ON and OFF signals, called digital data, and how basic building blocks called logic gates are used to perform operations. Students will use a tool “LogiSim” for building logic circuits. Second, we will discover how software is created step by step through a process called the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), and we will compare two popular approaches - the Waterfall model and the Agile model using real examples. Finally, we will learn how computers and devices communicate with each other over a network, including a well- known seven-layer model called the OSI model and the TCP/IP model that powers the internet. By the end of this unit, we will have a clear understanding of how computers think, how software is built, and how devices talk to each other. 1.1.1 Discrete and Continuous Quantities: In our daily life, we deal with two types of quantities: discrete and continuous. Examples include: ¢ Number of students in a classroom ¢ Number of books on a shelf e¢ Number of cars in a parking lot e Number of fingers on our hand Continuous quantities can take any value within a range. It was invented by Maurice Karnaugh in 1953. K-maps help us reduce the number of logic gates needed in a circuit, making circuits simpler, cheaper, and faster. Why Use K-Maps? When we have a Boolean expression with many terms, simplifying it using Boolean algebra can be difficult and time-consuming. K-maps provide a visual and systematic method to find the simplest form. Benefits of K-Maps: e Easier than algebraic simplification e Visual method - you can see patterns e Always gives the simplest result e Reduces errors e Works well for 2, 3, and 4 variables Structure of K-Maps: A K-map is a grid where: B=0 B-1 e Each cell represents one row of the e Adjacent cells differ by only one variable (Gray code order) A=1 e Adjacent cells, including wrapping around with a | can be grouped to simplify expressions. In general, we can make groups of 2” cells (1, 2, 4, 8...), where n> 0. Make as large as possible groups of cells, even if the groups are overlapping. Important Rule: In K-maps, cells that are next to each other (including wrapping around edges) differ by only ONE bit. This is called Gray code arrangement. ‘cA 4 mad Rae \ X
